screens.title: Understanding Load Balancers: Types and Algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll understand what a load balancer does and why it’s essential for any horizontally scaled system. Think of a load balancer as a traffic cop that directs requests to a pool of backend servers, keeping any one server from becoming a bottleneck. You’ll learn the practical differences between Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancers, the common algorithms used to choose a backend, and the operational features—like health checks, SSL termination, and session persistence—that make load balancers more than simple routers. We’ll ground these ideas with concrete examples: when a fast, transport-layer decision is enough, and when application-aware routing is required in microservices. You’ll also see a starter Nginx configuration you can adapt and test in a staging environment. By the end of this chapter, you’ll be able to match application needs to the right load balancer type and pick an algorithm that avoids common pitfalls such as uneven load distribution or sticky-session churn.

screens.title: What is a Load Balancer?
screens.narratorSegment: A load balancer is a device or software component that distributes incoming network traffic across multiple backend servers to prevent any single server from becoming overloaded. Its primary goals are maximizing resource utilization, reducing response time, and improving fault tolerance. Think of it like a traffic cop at an intersection: the cop ensures vehicles flow smoothly to multiple lanes so one lane does not jam. In practice, the load balancer accepts client connections and forwards requests to one of the servers in a backend pool, often performing health checks and removing servers that fail checks. A concrete example: a web application with three identical servers behind a load balancer will keep serving users even if one server crashes, because health checks will detect the failure and stop sending traffic to it. A common misconception is that a load balancer just forwards packets without intelligence. In reality, modern load balancers include features such as SSL termination, session persistence, and content-based routing that add operational flexibility. Key takeaway: a load balancer is both a distribution mechanism and a resilience layer; when you design systems you must specify health checks and routing behavior to maintain user experience during failures.

keyIdea.text: A load balancer distributes requests to maximize utilization and protect availability; it's more than packet forwarding.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is a Load Balancer?
Core Concept

Load Balancer: definition & goals

A component that directs requests across multiple servers to avoid overload, improve response times, and increase fault tolerance.

Health checks remove failing servers automatically.
SSL termination can offload CPU work from the backends.
Session persistence keeps stateful clients on a single backend.
Key Takeaway

A load balancer is the operational gateway that balances traffic and enforces health-driven routing to maintain availability.

Analogy & Example
Analogy
Traffic cop directing cars to lanes

The cop ensures even flow and removes blocked lanes. Similarly, a load balancer routes requests and excludes unhealthy servers.

Concrete example
Three web servers behind a balancer

If one server crashes, health checks remove it so users continue to be served by the remaining servers without manual intervention.

Common misconception
A load balancer is not just a dumb forwarder; modern ones provide TLS offload, persistence, and content-based routing that affect architecture.

screens.title: Operational Features of Load Balancers
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond simple request distribution, load balancers provide operational features that shape reliability and user experience. Health checks probe backend endpoints and remove servers that do not respond correctly. This means failed nodes stop receiving traffic until they recover, preventing user requests from hitting broken services. SSL or TLS termination at the load balancer offloads expensive encryption and decryption from the backend, simplifying certificate management and improving backend throughput. Session persistence, sometimes called sticky sessions, keeps a client bound to the same backend—useful for stateful applications but risky if a backend fails and state is lost. Content-based routing inspects application-level data like URL paths or headers to forward requests to specialized services; for example, requests for /api/users could route to a user service while /api/products goes elsewhere. A common mistake is to rely on sticky sessions for scale without designing for server failure and state replication. Another is placing TLS termination without considering end-to-end security policies. In short, configure these features deliberately and test their interplay in staging. Operational Features of Load Balancers means health checks, tls termination, persistence, and content routing are core features that affect reliability and design.. In practical terms, health checks, ssl termination, session persistence, and content routing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Operational Features
Definition

Key operational capabilities

Health checks
Periodic probes that verify a server’s availability. Failed checks remove servers until recovery.
SSL/TLS termination
Offloads encryption work to the balancer and centralizes certificate management.
Session persistence
Keeps a client routed to the same backend for stateful interactions; plan for failure handling.
Content-based routing
Use HTTP headers, paths, or cookies to route to service-specific backends in microservices.
Example & Guidance
Example
API gateway style routing

An L7 load balancer terminates TLS, inspects the path, and forwards /api/users to a user service while offloading TLS so backends receive plain HTTP locally.

Common mistake
Enabling sticky sessions without state replication: when the sticky backend fails, user state is lost and sessions break.
Key Takeaway

Operational features greatly affect architecture and fault handling; configure and test them deliberately.

screens.title: Starter Nginx Upstream Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: We now look at a practical Nginx example that demonstrates upstream configuration for load balancing. The upstream block lists backend servers and optionally configures the algorithm. By default Nginx uses Round Robin, so no directive is needed for that behavior. To select Least Connections, add least_conn inside the upstream block. In the server block you proxy_pass requests to the named upstream; typical headers such as Host and X-Forwarded-For are forwarded to preserve client information. A concrete test you can run locally uses three simple servers on ports 8081, 8082, and 8083. Start them and issue repeated requests to observe distribution. A common pitfall is editing an upstream without reloading Nginx correctly or forgetting to test health check behavior; in production you should reload with zero-downtime and validate changes in staging. This example translates the algorithms we’ll study into a concrete configuration you can modify and test. keyIdea.title: Nginx example
keyIdea.text: Round Robin is default; add least_conn to upstream to use Least Connections. Proxy headers preserve client context.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Nginx Upstream
Code Walkthrough
# Nginx configuration for load balancing
worker_processes auto;

events {
  worker_connections 1024;
}

http {
  upstream backend_servers {
    server 127.0.0.1:8081;
    server 127.0.0.1:8082;
    server 127.0.0.1:8083;
    # For Least Connections add:
    # least_conn;
  }

  server {
    listen 80;
    server_name localhost;

    location / {
      proxy_pass http://backend_servers;
      proxy_set_header Host $host;
      proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
      proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    }
  }
}
Guidance & Example
To observe behavior locally, run three simple web servers on ports 8081, 8082, 8083 and reload Nginx after each config edit. For Round Robin no explicit directive is needed; to switch to Least Connections, add least_conn; to weight servers, use server ... weight=3 in the upstream block.
Common pitfall: forgetting to forward X-Forwarded-For results in lost client IP context used by logging or IP-based algorithms.
Try this

Start simple servers and compare request distribution after toggling least_conn in the upstream block.

screens.title: Layer 4 (L4) Load Balancers
screens.narratorSegment: Layer 4 load balancers operate at the transport layer and make routing decisions using IP addresses and port numbers. They forward TCP or UDP packets and generally do not inspect application payloads. Because they work with lower-layer headers only, L4 balancers are fast and introduce minimal processing overhead. They are a good fit for high-throughput services where content-based routing is unnecessary, for example certain database proxies, real-time gaming servers, or simple HTTP services that do not need application-level routing. A concrete example: using HAProxy in TCP mode to distribute database connections across replicas. One common misconception is that L4 is always 'simpler' to operate; while it avoids application-level inspection, it also cannot provide features like URL-based routing or TLS offload at the HTTP level. If your architecture needs path-based routing, routing by hostname, or inspection of headers for security rules, you should consider an L7 solution. Key takeaway: choose L4 when throughput and low latency matter and when application-aware routing is not required. In practical terms, transport-layer routing: speed, simplicity, and use cases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Layer 4 (L4)
Definition

Layer 4 load balancers

Operate on TCP/UDP headers and forward packets based on IP and port, avoiding application-layer inspection for minimal overhead.

Fast and efficient for high-throughput services.
Cannot route by URL path or headers.
Useful where TLS termination at L7 is not required.
Examples and Misconception
Example
HAProxy in TCP mode for database proxies

Distributes connection-level traffic without inspecting SQL or HTTP payloads, keeping latency low.

Misconception: L4 can't be used with TLS. In fact, L4 can forward encrypted connections, but it cannot perform HTTP-level routing or TLS-aware content inspection.
Key Takeaway

Pick L4 for raw speed and when routing decisions only need transport headers.

screens.title: Layer 7 (L7) Load Balancers
screens.narratorSegment: Layer 7 load balancers work at the application layer and terminate the client connection so they can inspect full HTTP requests, including headers, cookies, URL paths, and sometimes body content. This enables content-based routing: forward /api/users to a user service and /api/products to a product service. L7 balancers can also perform TLS termination, request compression, caching, and simple content modification. The trade-off is additional processing overhead and a small latency increase compared with L4. L7 is essential for modern web applications and microservices where routing decisions depend on HTTP semantics. For example, an Nginx or HAProxy in HTTP mode can inspect paths and headers to route requests to different backend pools. A common misconception is that L7 is always the better choice simply because it is more flexible; however, this flexibility comes at the cost of higher C P U usage and possible latency, so select L7 when your routing rules or features require application-layer information. Ultimately, L7 enables richer routing and features but must be justified by use case requirements. Layer 7 (L7) Load Balancers means l7 load balancers inspect http data for content-based routing and advanced features, trading some latency for flexibility.. In practical terms, application-layer routing: flexibility, inspection, and trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Layer 7 (L7)
Definition

Layer 7 load balancers

Terminate HTTP(S), inspect headers and paths, and route based on application data. Support TLS termination, caching, and content rules.

Content-based routing enables microservices mappings by path or header.
TLS termination centralizes certificates and offloads backend CPU.
Introduces modest processing latency compared to L4.
Example & Contrast
Example
Microservices behind an L7 balancer

The balancer inspects the path and routes requests for different API endpoints to their respective services, enabling a consolidated entry point for the application.

Contrast: Use L7 if you need URL path or header-based decisions; use L4 if only transport-level routing is sufficient and latency is critical.
Key Takeaway

L7 provides rich routing and operational features; choose it when application-layer context is needed.

screens.title: Comparing L4 and L7 Load Balancers
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between L4 and L7 involves weighing speed against routing intelligence. L4 operates on transport headers and is fast; L7 inspects HTTP content and enables features like content-based routing and TLS termination. To decide, ask: do routing rules depend on URL paths, headers, or cookies? If yes, L7 is required. Do you need the lowest possible latency and minimal processing overhead? If yes, favor L4. Also consider operational needs: centralized TLS certificates and application-layer security often push designs toward L7. A concrete decision checklist: use L4 for simple TCP/UDP services and high-throughput proxies; use L7 for microservices, A P I gateways, and content routing. A common trap is defaulting to L7 because of its flexibility; this can introduce unnecessary C P U overhead and cost. Another consideration is the ability to perform health checks that understand application semantics—L7 checks can validate an HTTP response body or status code, while L4 checks usually confirm connection-level health. The key is matching your application's routing needs to the balancer’s capabilities and validating the decision under representative load. In practical terms, feature comparison and decision checklist. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › L4 vs L7 Comparison
Quick Comparison
L4
Transport-level, low latency, no HTTP inspection.
L7
Application-level, content routing, TLS termination.
Use case

screens.title: Round Robin and Weighted Round Robin
screens.narratorSegment: Round Robin is the simplest load balancing algorithm: requests are sent to backends in sequence and then the sequence repeats. It assumes servers have similar capacity and request processing time. A concrete example: with three servers, server one gets request one, server two gets request two, and so on. The limitation is that it does not account for long-running requests or uneven server capacity. Weighted Round Robin improves this by assigning a numeric weight to each server so more powerful servers receive proportionally more requests. For example, a server with weight three receives three times the requests of a server with weight one. This is useful for heterogeneous pools where servers differ in C P U or memory. A common misconception is that weighting solves all imbalance problems; it only helps when capacity estimates are stable. If request times vary wildly or if backends experience transient slowdowns, dynamic algorithms like Least Connections may perform better. When implementing weighted schemes, monitor actual throughput and adjust weights based on observed performance, not just on nominal hardware specs. Round Robin and Weighted Round Robin means round robin is simple and fair for equal servers; weighted round robin adjusts for capacity differences but needs tuning.. In practical terms, sequential distribution and capacity-aware weighting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Algorithm

Round Robin

Distributes requests sequentially across servers. Simple and predictable when servers are equal.

Scenario
Three identical backends receiving evenly spaced requests will get roughly equal traffic with Round Robin.
Algorithm

Weighted Round Robin

Assign weights to servers so more capable servers receive more requests; useful for heterogeneous fleets.

Guidance
Set weights based on observed capacity and adjust after measuring throughput under load.
Misconception: weights don't adapt dynamically to transient load. Combine with health checks and monitoring for robust behavior.

screens.title: Least Connections and Least Response Time
screens.narratorSegment: Least Connections directs new requests to the backend with the fewest active connections. It is dynamic and adapts to varying connection durations, making it effective for workloads where connection time varies widely, such as long-lived WebSocket connections. A practical example is a chat service where some connections are long-lived; Least Connections prevents a server with many long-standing sessions from receiving even more new ones. Least Response Time sends traffic to the server with the fastest response or lowest latency, often using health check and telemetry data. This can favor geographically closer or less loaded servers. A common misconception is that dynamic algorithms remove the need for health checks—this is false. Both Least Connections and Least Response Time benefit from accurate health checks and telemetry because they rely on current-state information. Implement these algorithms when you need responsiveness to runtime conditions, but ensure your monitoring and metric collection are reliable and low-latency so the algorithm makes correct decisions. Least Connections and Least Response Time means least connections and least response time adapt to real-time server load and latency; they rely on accurate health and telemetry.. In practical terms, dynamic algorithms that consider current load and latency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: IP Hash and Session Persistence
screens.narratorSegment: IP Hash uses a hash of the client IP address to deterministically select a backend, ensuring the same client IP usually goes to the same server. This provides a way to achieve session persistence without cookies, but it relies on the client IP remaining stable. A concrete example is a legacy web app that stores session state in-memory on a server; IP Hash keeps a returning client on the same server. A major limitation is that many clients sit behind NATs or proxies where many users share an IP, which can create hotspots. Another problem is mobile clients whose IPs change as they move networks, breaking persistence. Session persistence alternatives include cookie-based stickiness or designing the application to be stateless and store session state in a shared store, avoiding stickiness entirely. A common misconception is that IP Hash balances evenly—if client IP distribution is skewed, the distribution will be skewed too. Use IP Hash only when you understand client IP characteristics and have considered failure modes. IP Hash and Session Persistence means ip hash provides deterministic client routing but depends on ip stability and uniform client-ip distribution.. In practical terms, consistent routing for clients and limits of ip-based stickiness. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Definition

IP Hash

Use a hash of the client IP to route consistently to one backend, supporting session persistence without cookies.

When to use
Legacy apps with in-memory sessions and stable client IPs may benefit; otherwise prefer stateless design or cookie stickiness.
Limitations & Example
Example
In-memory session app

IP Hash keeps a returning client routed to the same server, but if the client IP changes, session affinity breaks.

Common mistake: assuming IP Hash balances evenly across a user base. If many users share a NATed IP, that IP gets disproportionate load.

screens.title: How Algorithms Affect Performance and Distribution
screens.narratorSegment: Each load balancing algorithm shapes how traffic and load concentrate across backends, which directly affects latency, resource utilization, and fault behavior. Round Robin gives predictable sequence-based distribution but ignores runtime load; if requests vary in duration, some servers can become overloaded. Weighted Round Robin compensates for different server capacities but needs accurate weight tuning that reflects observed throughput. Least Connections reacts to runtime load by favoring servers with fewer active connections, which helps when connection durations vary widely; however, inaccurate tracking of active connections or rapid connection churn can mislead the algorithm. Least Response Time prefers lower-latency servers, which is useful when you have geographically dispersed backends or varying network conditions, but it relies on timely latency metrics and good health data. IP Hash gives consistency per-client IP but can create hotspots if client IPs are unevenly distributed. Operationally, misconfiguring the algorithm or omitting health checks can create hotspots or route traffic to slow or failed servers. The practical guidance is to pick an algorithm aligned with your workload profile, instrument active metrics, and validate behavior under staged traffic. screens.title: Choosing the Right Type and Algorithm
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting the right load balancer and algorithm requires mapping your application’s characteristics to the balancer’s strengths. First, identify whether routing decisions must use application-layer data like paths or headers. If they do, pick an L7 balancer; if not, an L4 balancer can offer lower latency. Second, profile your workload: if connections vary in length or you have long-lived connections, choose Least Connections. If servers have differing capacities, consider Weighted Round Robin. If you require client affinity and can tolerate IP-based limitations, IP Hash is an option, though cookie-based persistence or stateless design is often preferable. Always enable health checks that match the expected application semantics, and instrument the system to gather active connections, response times, and error rates. Validate your configuration in a staging environment by simulating realistic traffic, including failure scenarios, to see how the balancer responds. screens.narratorSegment: Let’s apply these ideas to two scenarios from the chapter. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll understand what a load balancer does and why it’s essential for any horizontally scaled system. Think of a load balancer as a traffic cop that directs requests to a pool of backend servers, keeping any one server from becoming a bottleneck. You’ll learn the practical differences between Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancers, the common algorithms used to choose a backend, and the operational features—like health checks, SSL termination, and session persistence—that make load balancers more than simple routers. We’ll ground these ideas with concrete examples: when a fast, transport-layer decision is enough, and when application-aware routing is required in microservices. You’ll also see a starter Nginx configuration you can adapt and test in a staging environment. By the end of this chapter, you’ll be able to match application needs to the right load balancer type and pick an algorithm that avoids common pitfalls such as uneven load distribution or sticky-session churn.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the purpose of a load balancer in a horizontally scaled system, choose between Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancers based on application needs, and describe the mechanics of several common load balancing algorithms. You will practice reading a starter Nginx configuration, toggle between Round Robin and Least Connections, and reason about how algorithm choice affects latency and throughput. The objectives emphasize practical judgment: when to offload TLS, when session persistence is required, and how health checks prevent user-visible failures. Each objective connects to a hands-on task or scenario so you gain competence, not just vocabulary. You’ll also learn to spot common misconfigurations that can cause uneven load or downtime, and to run tests in a staging environment before production rollout. This chapter teaches both the conceptual model and the decision-making steps you’ll use as an engineer.

This second set of objectives focuses on hands-on practice and interpretation. You will edit an Nginx upstream block to toggle between Round Robin and Least Connections and run simple local web servers to observe distribution. You’ll configure basic health checks and see how automatic removal and reinsertion of backends changes request routing. You will practice enabling TLS termination on the load balancer to offload C P U work from backends and test session persistence strategies for stateful flows. These tasks train you to reason about the operational effects of configuration changes before you deploy them. The practice emphasizes measurable checks: observe active connections, measure response time, and confirm that content-based routing goes to the intended service. With these exercises you move from conceptual understanding to applied configuration and validation. Learning Objectives — Practical Tasks means practice nginx configuration, health checks, tls termination, and session persistence validation.. In practical terms, hands-on skills and checks you will practice. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A load balancer is a device or software component that distributes incoming network traffic across multiple backend servers to prevent any single server from becoming overloaded. Its primary goals are maximizing resource utilization, reducing response time, and improving fault tolerance. Think of it like a traffic cop at an intersection: the cop ensures vehicles flow smoothly to multiple lanes so one lane does not jam. In practice, the load balancer accepts client connections and forwards requests to one of the servers in a backend pool, often performing health checks and removing servers that fail checks. A concrete example: a web application with three identical servers behind a load balancer will keep serving users even if one server crashes, because health checks will detect the failure and stop sending traffic to it. A common misconception is that a load balancer just forwards packets without intelligence. In reality, modern load balancers include features such as SSL termination, session persistence, and content-based routing that add operational flexibility. Key takeaway: a load balancer is both a distribution mechanism and a resilience layer; when you design systems you must specify health checks and routing behavior to maintain user experience during failures.

Beyond simple request distribution, load balancers provide operational features that shape reliability and user experience. Health checks probe backend endpoints and remove servers that do not respond correctly. This means failed nodes stop receiving traffic until they recover, preventing user requests from hitting broken services. SSL or TLS termination at the load balancer offloads expensive encryption and decryption from the backend, simplifying certificate management and improving backend throughput. Session persistence, sometimes called sticky sessions, keeps a client bound to the same backend—useful for stateful applications but risky if a backend fails and state is lost. Content-based routing inspects application-level data like URL paths or headers to forward requests to specialized services; for example, requests for /api/users could route to a user service while /api/products goes elsewhere. A common mistake is to rely on sticky sessions for scale without designing for server failure and state replication. Another is placing TLS termination without considering end-to-end security policies. In short, configure these features deliberately and test their interplay in staging. Layer 4 load balancers operate at the transport layer and make routing decisions using IP addresses and port numbers. They forward TCP or UDP packets and generally do not inspect application payloads. Because they work with lower-layer headers only, L4 balancers are fast and introduce minimal processing overhead. They are a good fit for high-throughput services where content-based routing is unnecessary, for example certain database proxies, real-time gaming servers, or simple HTTP services that do not need application-level routing. A concrete example: using HAProxy in TCP mode to distribute database connections across replicas. One common misconception is that L4 is always 'simpler' to operate; while it avoids application-level inspection, it also cannot provide features like URL-based routing or TLS offload at the HTTP level. If your architecture needs path-based routing, routing by hostname, or inspection of headers for security rules, you should consider an L7 solution. Key takeaway: choose L4 when throughput and low latency matter and when application-aware routing is not required. Layer 7 load balancers work at the application layer and terminate the client connection so they can inspect full HTTP requests, including headers, cookies, URL paths, and sometimes body content. This enables content-based routing: forward /api/users to a user service and /api/products to a product service. L7 balancers can also perform TLS termination, request compression, caching, and simple content modification. The trade-off is additional processing overhead and a small latency increase compared with L4. L7 is essential for modern web applications and microservices where routing decisions depend on HTTP semantics. For example, an Nginx or HAProxy in HTTP mode can inspect paths and headers to route requests to different backend pools. A common misconception is that L7 is always the better choice simply because it is more flexible; however, this flexibility comes at the cost of higher C P U usage and possible latency, so select L7 when your routing rules or features require application-layer information. Choosing between L4 and L7 involves weighing speed against routing intelligence. L4 operates on transport headers and is fast; L7 inspects HTTP content and enables features like content-based routing and TLS termination. To decide, ask: do routing rules depend on URL paths, headers, or cookies? If yes, L7 is required. Do you need the lowest possible latency and minimal processing overhead? If yes, favor L4. Also consider operational needs: centralized TLS certificates and application-layer security often push designs toward L7. A concrete decision checklist: use L4 for simple TCP/UDP services and high-throughput proxies; use L7 for microservices, A P I gateways, and content routing. A common trap is defaulting to L7 because of its flexibility; this can introduce unnecessary C P U overhead and cost. Another consideration is the ability to perform health checks that understand application semantics—L7 checks can validate an HTTP response body or status code, while L4 checks usually confirm connection-level health. The key is matching your application's routing needs to the balancer’s capabilities and validating the decision under representative load. Round Robin is the simplest load balancing algorithm: requests are sent to backends in sequence and then the sequence repeats. It assumes servers have similar capacity and request processing time. A concrete example: with three servers, server one gets request one, server two gets request two, and so on. The limitation is that it does not account for long-running requests or uneven server capacity. Weighted Round Robin improves this by assigning a numeric weight to each server so more powerful servers receive proportionally more requests. For example, a server with weight three receives three times the requests of a server with weight one. This is useful for heterogeneous pools where servers differ in C P U or memory. A common misconception is that weighting solves all imbalance problems; it only helps when capacity estimates are stable. If request times vary wildly or if backends experience transient slowdowns, dynamic algorithms like Least Connections may perform better. When implementing weighted schemes, monitor actual throughput and adjust weights based on observed performance, not just on nominal hardware specs. Least Connections directs new requests to the backend with the fewest active connections. It is dynamic and adapts to varying connection durations, making it effective for workloads where connection time varies widely, such as long-lived WebSocket connections. A practical example is a chat service where some connections are long-lived; Least Connections prevents a server with many long-standing sessions from receiving even more new ones. Least Response Time sends traffic to the server with the fastest response or lowest latency, often using health check and telemetry data. This can favor geographically closer or less loaded servers. A common misconception is that dynamic algorithms remove the need for health checks—this is false. Both Least Connections and Least Response Time benefit from accurate health checks and telemetry because they rely on current-state information. Implement these algorithms when you need responsiveness to runtime conditions, but ensure your monitoring and metric collection are reliable and low-latency so the algorithm makes correct decisions. IP Hash uses a hash of the client IP address to deterministically select a backend, ensuring the same client IP usually goes to the same server. This provides a way to achieve session persistence without cookies, but it relies on the client IP remaining stable. A concrete example is a legacy web app that stores session state in-memory on a server; IP Hash keeps a returning client on the same server. A major limitation is that many clients sit behind NATs or proxies where many users share an IP, which can create hotspots. Another problem is mobile clients whose IPs change as they move networks, breaking persistence. Session persistence alternatives include cookie-based stickiness or designing the application to be stateless and store session state in a shared store, avoiding stickiness entirely. A common misconception is that IP Hash balances evenly—if client IP distribution is skewed, the distribution will be skewed too. Use IP Hash only when you understand client IP characteristics and have considered failure modes. Each load balancing algorithm shapes how traffic and load concentrate across backends, which directly affects latency, resource utilization, and fault behavior. Round Robin gives predictable sequence-based distribution but ignores runtime load; if requests vary in duration, some servers can become overloaded. Weighted Round Robin compensates for different server capacities but needs accurate weight tuning that reflects observed throughput. Least Connections reacts to runtime load by favoring servers with fewer active connections, which helps when connection durations vary widely; however, inaccurate tracking of active connections or rapid connection churn can mislead the algorithm. Least Response Time prefers lower-latency servers, which is useful when you have geographically dispersed backends or varying network conditions, but it relies on timely latency metrics and good health data. IP Hash gives consistency per-client IP but can create hotspots if client IPs are unevenly distributed. Operationally, misconfiguring the algorithm or omitting health checks can create hotspots or route traffic to slow or failed servers. Selecting the right load balancer and algorithm requires mapping your application’s characteristics to the balancer’s strengths. First, identify whether routing decisions must use application-layer data like paths or headers. If they do, pick an L7 balancer; if not, an L4 balancer can offer lower latency. Second, profile your workload: if connections vary in length or you have long-lived connections, choose Least Connections. If servers have differing capacities, consider Weighted Round Robin. If you require client affinity and can tolerate IP-based limitations, IP Hash is an option, though cookie-based persistence or stateless design is often preferable. Always enable health checks that match the expected application semantics, and instrument the system to gather active connections, response times, and error rates. Validate your configuration in a staging environment by simulating realistic traffic, including failure scenarios, to see how the balancer responds.
